channel.title: Networking II: VLANs, DNS, DHCP :: School-related IT Infrastructure
channel.description: Self-study · no session of its own · not graded · Time needed: approx. 2 hours of theory, optionally approx. 2 hours of lab Self-study This chapter has no session in the timetable and no homework or graded submission. You work through it on your own. It is the basis for chapter 4 (server roles) on 16.11. and 23.11.2026: if you take on the DHCP, DNS or directory service role there, read the corresponding theory sections beforehand.

item.title: Learning goals
item.description: After this chapter you can: explain why a school network is divided into VLANs (separating groups, smaller broadcast domains, flexibility without additional hardware), describe the difference between an access port and a trunk port and explain what the 802.1Q tag in an Ethernet frame contains, justify why devices in different VLANs can only talk to each other via a router (or layer-3 switch) and why permission or denial is decided there: a VLAN separates, an access rule permits, read a permission matrix (who may reach which service in which network) and translate it into access rules, explain the DHCP sequence (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge), the most important DHCP options and the job of a DHCP relay, describe the path of a DNS query from the device via the resolver to the responsible server and distinguish the record types A, AAAA, PTR, CNAME, MX and SRV, use dig, getent, /etc/resolv.conf (Linux) as well as ipconfig /all, nslookup and Resolve-DnsName (Windows) to find out which address, which DNS server and which gateway a device uses, explain how a captive portal in the guest Wi-Fi works. Mapping to the competency list: to follow (placeholder).

item.title: Theory
item.description: VLANs: several networks on the same switches The problem with a flat network In the Packet Tracer network from session 2, every group had its own switch: sw-verw, sw-lehr, sw-srv. That works for three groups in one room. A real school, however, has eight or more groups (see the IP plan of Mittelschule Musterstadt: administration, teachers, student Wi-Fi, servers, computer lab, guest Wi-Fi, printers, network management), and on every floor there are devices from almost all groups.

item.title: Lab with solutions (optional)
item.description: Optional, not graded This lab is optional. There is nothing to submit. Every task has a solution you can expand. Try it yourself first, then compare. Status: untested The commands have not yet been run in Packet Tracer 9.0.1 or in the course environment. Tested on: open. Overview Part Content Duration Prerequisite 1 VLANs in Packet Tracer: three groups on one switch, router on a stick approx. 50 min schulnetz.pkt from session 2 2 Permission matrix as an access rule (ACL) approx. 30 min Part 1 3 Observing DNS and DHCP in the Debian VM approx. 30 min VM debian-lab from session 1 Part 1: VLANs in Packet Tracer Goal: Instead of one switch per group, administration, teachers and students are connected to one switch in three VLANs. The router connects the VLANs over one cable (trunk) with subinterfaces.

item.title: Security and data protection
item.description: No legal advice This section gives technical orientation. Legal questions (e.g. logging, retention periods, youth protection filters) are clarified by the school with the data protection officer and the school maintainer. The essentials Topic Measure A VLAN is not a firewall Always apply access rules between VLANs according to the permission matrix. Without rules, every VLAN reaches every other one via the router. Native VLAN On trunks, do not use VLAN 1 as the untagged VLAN; use a separate, otherwise unused VLAN. This makes VLAN hopping harder (an attacker sends frames with two tags). Unused ports Shut them down (shutdown) and assign them to an unused VLAN. Network sockets in classrooms are freely accessible. No automatic trunks Configure ports to end devices explicitly as access ports (switchport mode access) so that no device can negotiate a trunk. Rogue DHCP servers DHCP snooping on the switch: DHCP replies only from the ports of the real servers. Network management Manage switches, access points and routers only from the management VLAN (99), never from the student or guest Wi-Fi. DNS resolver Answer recursive queries only from your own network, otherwise the server can be abused for attacks on third parties. Guest Wi-Fi Separate VLAN, internet only, devices isolated from each other. A captive portal encrypts nothing. Data protection in the school context DHCP logs show which device (MAC address, device name such as “Annas-Laptop”) was on the network when. That is personal data, students’ included. DNS logs show which sites were visited. They reveal more than many people think. Decide whether to log, who may see the logs and when they are deleted. DNS filters (e.g. for youth protection) are common. They should be transparent: students and parents should know that filtering happens and by which rules. Captive portals with registration (name, e-mail, phone number) collect data. Ask only for what is necessary and delete the data after a short time.
